lines: Comparing a row to its own neighbors is one kind of question. Now comparing a row to the exact value another table held, at that very moment in time.
Look at the timeline. Prices change on three days, and four orders land between them.
An order on day twelve must be matched to the price that was in effect on day twelve. Not the first price, and not today's.
The question is about a moment, and that is not a question a plain join was designed to answer.
See what a plain join does. It matches on the product alone, so every order meets every price.
Count the lines: four orders, three prices, twelve pairings. Almost all of them are wrong.
The data is fine. The matching rule just has no notion of before and after.
The natural repair is to add a condition: the price must have started on or before the order.
Run it in your head against the four orders. Count the prices that satisfy the condition for each.
How many rows survive?
answer: Seven. One, one, two and three.
The inequality removed the prices from the future, but every older price still qualifies. The order on day twelve matches both the first price and the second.
Twelve is the unfiltered product, and four is what we actually want. The missing step is to keep only the closest.

lines: So the rule has three parts. Equality on the product narrows the candidates. An inequality on time removes the future. And of what is left, the latest one wins.
Watch the thick lines: each order points at the nearest earlier price, and nothing else.
That shape is called an as of join. Exactly one row per order, which is the number you started with.
You can write that rule with tools you already have. A subquery ordered by start date, newest first, cut off at one row.
Or the lateral form with the same ending, which you met two topics ago.
Both are cheap only if an index on the product and the start date lets each lookup jump straight to the right place.
Without that index, every order rescans the whole history, which is the quadratic habit from the window internals topic.
Several engines have the operator built in. Read the three spellings.
They differ in punctuation but not in meaning. An inequality, and each left row joins at most one right row, the closest.
Snowflake adds a named clause for the comparison, so the as of condition is separate from the plain equality.
Where you have the native form, use it. It says what you mean.
Edge case. An order is placed on day zero, before the product's first price existed.
Think about what the closest earlier price is.
What does the left version of the join return for that order?
answer: The order, with a missing price.
There is nothing to match, and a left join keeps the left row with nulls on the right. An inner version would drop the order entirely.
It does not invent the first price, because that price did not yet exist, and it does not raise an error.

lines: The native operator also plans differently. Watch the two rows.
Both inputs are naturally in time order, so the engine can walk them together in one pass.
The hand built forms seek once per order, and that is what the nested loop line shows.
That is why one engine lists the operator as supported only by specific algorithms: it has a dedicated path, not the general join machinery.
Here is why this matters beyond reports. Suppose you train a model, and one feature is the price.
Join a training example from day five to today's price, and the example has seen eleven, a value that did not exist on day five.
The model learns from the future. Offline accuracy looks wonderful, and production fails, because the future is not available there.
The as of value is ten, and the as of join gives you that by construction. That is how you build a training set without leakage.
One last wrinkle. Everything so far used a single axis of time: when the fact was true.
Look at the second axis. A bitemporal system also records when the database learned the fact.
That matters when a correction arrives late. The question becomes: as of the time we asked, what did we believe was true at the earlier time.
It is a harder problem, and it gets its own chapter. Know it exists, and do not reach for it unless the requirement has two independent axes.
To sum up. Use the native operator where the engine has one, and an indexed lateral where it does not.
Audit every join to a current value in a feature pipeline, because that is where leakage hides.
Every clause so far answered what a query means. Next: what actually happens between typing that query and getting an answer back.
Two checks. First, is an as of join just an equi join with extra steps.
Is it an equi join?
answer: It uses equality to narrow the candidates, but it needs an inequality on time and a closest wins rule to choose one. An equi join alone cannot say before or after.

lines: Second check. In Snowflake, the as of comparison is named in its own clause.
Which clause?
answer: It sits apart from the ordinary equality condition, so the join says separately which columns must be equal and which must be ordered.
